item.title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Spin-completed post-processing of qDRIFT measurement samples eliminates spin contamination, giving subspace roots with spin error |⟨Sˆ2⟩−S(S+1)|<10−11. On an IBM Heron processor, it matches Cartesian post-processing accuracy while reducing diagonalized subspace dimensions by two to three orders of magnitude.

Grade 0.382 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Stefano Barison, Samuele Piccinelli, Alberto Baiardi, Francesco Tacchino, Ivano Tavernelli

Figure

Energy error relative to DMRG (top) and total spin deviation |⟨Sˆ2⟩−S(S+1)| (bottom) versus diagonalized subspace dimension for singlet, triplet, and quintet states of oxo-Mn(Salen). Spin completion maintains exact spin purity and reaches target energy accuracy with subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than Cartesian post-processing.

Asks

How can spin symmetry be incorporated into sample-based quantum diagonalization pipelines based on randomized time evolution?

But

Demonstrated on active spaces up to (32e, 24o). Spin completion requires enumerating all open-shell spin couplings for sampled configurations, which scales exponentially with the count of singly occupied orbitals.

Tools

SqDRIFT · configuration state function (CSF) completion · IBM Heron r3 (ibm_boston) · SBD selected subspace diagonalizer · configuration recovery

Abstract

Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under hatS², and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an [Fe(NH₃)₄]²⁺ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.

item.title: Compiling Matrix Formulas to Quantum Block Encodings
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Synthesizes quantum block-encoding circuits directly from matrix entry formulas, matching or beating 37 of 39 published baselines and improving subnormalization by up to 10,487× in under 5 seconds for dimensions exceeding 2100.

Grade 0.373 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Daksh Shami, Charles Yuan

Figure

Total MARBLE compile time (seconds) on the y-axis broken down by phase across matrix dimension N up to 2100 on the x-axis for three benchmark matrices. Circuit optimization time remains flat, keeping total execution under 5 seconds.

Asks

Can quantum block-encoding circuits be automatically synthesized with poly-logarithmic cost directly from mathematical entry formulas rather than designed by hand?

Before

Hand-crafted circuits or explicit entry enumeration like FABLE (Camps and Van Beeumen 2022), which incurs O(N2) gates and cannot scale past dimension ∼212×212.

But

Counts in Clifford+T+Rz gate set, treating arbitrary Rz gates as incurring O(log⁡(1/ϵ)) T gates. Hand-written rewrite rules capped at an intermediate representation size of 105 nodes.

Tools

equality saturation (e-graphs) · static multiplicity type checking · symbolic matrix forms · OpenQASM circuit synthesis

Abstract

Realizing the promise of quantum applications such as chemistry or fluid dynamics requires building quantum circuits that efficiently encode and manipulate exponentially large matrices. This process forces researchers to grapple with the reality that a matrix expressible as one equation on paper can map to thousands of bit-level quantum logic gates, historically written by hand. Even worse, it often ends with a discovery that the needed resources grow so quickly with matrix size that the quantum algorithm loses its asymptotic speedup. In this work, we present MARBLE, a language that automatically synthesizes an efficient circuit from the publication-style formula for the entries of a matrix. MARBLE algebraically rewrites programs into symbolic combinations of simpler matrices that have known circuit realizations. It analyzes costs of possible representations, notably the subnormalization term that dominates time complexity. It then emits an OpenQASM circuit and certifies whether its cost is poly-logarithmic in problem size, as required by quantum algorithms. When evaluated on quantum applications ranging from fluid dynamics to physical Hamiltonians, MARBLE matches or surpasses 37 of 39 published baselines. On the low end, it automatically matches many theoretically optimal circuits, and on the high end, it improves on a published construction in fluid dynamics by 10,487x in subnormalization. MARBLE produces exponentially smaller circuits than the leading tool FABLE, and it successfully compiles matrices whose dimensions exceed 2^100 within five seconds on a laptop.

item.title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Explicit normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix for 2D isotropic linear elasticity using a constant number of ancillae and logarithmic gate complexity in the degrees of freedom (44(nx+ny)+156 Hadamard, 48(nx+ny)+278 CNOT, 106(nx+ny)+341 T, and 64 Ry gates). Enables QSVT-based linear equation solving scaling as O~(κ).

Grade 0.370 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Yuki Sato, Ruho Kondo

Figure

Quantum circuit schematic implementing the normalized block encoding 𝐔B=𝐔L†𝐑L,out𝐔L for the shifted stiffness matrix, displaying register allocations across n=nx+ny system qubits and auxiliary registers.

Asks

Can finite element stiffness matrices for isotropic linear elasticity be efficiently block-encoded in a normalized, shifted form to enable square-root condition-number scaling O~(κ) in quantum linear system algorithms?

Before

Existing quantum finite element methods block-encode standard operators with query complexity linear in the condition number κ, whereas optimal positive-definite quantum solvers require normalized block-encodings of shifted operators (Orsucci and Dunjko 2021) which are not directly provided by standard block-encodings.

But

Restricted to 2D isotropic linear elastic materials on uniform rectangular meshes; requires condition number bounds or heuristic extrapolation to set polynomial degree; boundary and material oracles excluded from core gate count.

Tools

finite element method (Q₁ elements) · factorized finite element assembly · Gram matrix block-encoding · quantum singular value transformation (QSVT)

Abstract

Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

item.title: Entanglement and information dynamics in charged dual-unitary circuits with impurities
item.description:
Worth a look new result — A symmetry-breaking impurity in a charged dual-unitary quantum circuit generates persistent, non-vanishing stationary entanglement negativity and mutual information between intervals straddling the defect. It also violates the standard integrable identity ℰA1:A2=12ℐA1:A2(1/2).

Grade 0.352 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Shachar Fraenkel, Colin Rylands

Figure

Long-time asymptotic entanglement negativity ℰA1:A2(∞) and half Rényi mutual information 12ℐA1:A2(1/2)(∞) as a function of impurity parameter γ. Non-zero steady-state values persist across intermediate γ, and the two curves diverge, breaking the standard integrable equivalence.

Asks

How is non-equilibrium local relaxation and entanglement dynamics modified by a spatially fixed quantum impurity that breaks a global bulk symmetry outside the observed subsystem?

Before

In uncharged dual-unitary circuits or standard translation-invariant quenches, steady-state mutual information and negativity between separated intervals decay to zero, and the negativity satisfies ℰA1:A2=12ℐA1:A2(1/2).

But

Analytic derivations assume brickwork dual-unitary gates with chiral U(1)⊗U(1) symmetry, homogeneous initial states, and bulk dynamics either strictly non-interacting/integrable or chaotic (membrane picture).

Tools

Dual-unitary quantum circuits · Quasiparticle picture · Entanglement membrane picture · Replica trick with partial transpose

Abstract

Local parts of a closed, non-equilibrium quantum many-body system can reach stationarity through the buildup of entanglement between different regions. In this paper we investigate how this process is affected by the presence of a quantum impurity that breaks a global symmetry of the bulk. In particular, we study a charged dual-unitary quantum circuit perturbed by a symmetry-breaking, non-dual-unitary gate acting on a spatially fixed pair of sites. In this setup we calculate the entanglement entropy for a subsystem that does not contain the impurity, as well as the mutual information and logarithmic negativity for a bipartite subsystem that straddles the impurity. We obtain exact results in the early time regime for these quantities from the dual unitarity of the bulk system. Beyond this regime, we compute the predictions of the quasiparticle and entanglement membrane pictures, supporting them with exact calculations obtained by taking the corresponding limits of the bulk entangling power. We find that the presence of a symmetry-breaking impurity can lead to a richer behaviour of quantum relaxation, including non-monotonic evolution of the entanglement entropy, a modification of the long-time steady state, and persistent subsystem mutual information and entanglement negativity. This behaviour is understood in terms of long-range correlations generated by scattering from the impurity, and facilitated by the ballistic propagation of the conserved charges.

item.title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Demonstrates statistical quantum phase estimation on an analog simulator without auxiliary qubits, extracting absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in one- and two-dimensional arrays of up to N=19 Rydberg atoms.

Grade 0.340 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Hendrik Timme, Benjamin F. Schiffer, Ohad Lib, Shijia Sun, Maximilian Ammenwerth, Dominik S. Wild, J. Ignacio Cirac, Immanuel Bloch, Johannes Zeiher

Figure

Measured ground-state energy EGS/(NΩ) and separation to the first excited band versus detuning Δ/Ω for 5- and 19-atom chains, extracted from the Fourier transform of the reconstructed complex Loschmidt echo.

Asks

Can quantum phase estimation and complex-valued Loschmidt echoes be realized on an analog quantum simulator without controlled time evolution or ancilla registers?

But

Operates within the nearest-neighbor Rydberg blockade approximation (Vnn≫Ω,|Δ|); systematic phase error is 𝒪(τ2) after analytical initial-time bias subtraction, requiring nonzero echo amplitude.

Tools

Strontium-88 optical tweezer arrays · Clock-to-Rydberg transition (n=47 ³S₁) · Digital-analog imaginary-time evolution (ITE) protocol · Loschmidt echo phase reconstruction via Cauchy-Riemann relation · Statistical quantum phase estimation

Abstract

Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

item.title: Transfer-Matrix Calculus for Infinite Matrix Product States
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Ground-state extrapolation to zero energy variance per site gives nonzero charge-density-wave order m0=0.002213(14) in the half-filled 1/d Coulomb chain at weak coupling V=2, with variational energy variance down to 2×10−10.

Grade 0.340 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Qi Yang, Philippe Corboz

Figure

Energy per site e and charge-density-wave order parameter mCDW plotted against energy variance per site v for V=2 and V=4. Extrapolations to v→0 show finite charge order persisting down to V=2.

Asks

Can matrix product state algorithms compute thermodynamic-limit ground states, excitation spectra, and energy variances for algebraically decaying long-range interactions without fitting interactions to sums of exponentials?

Before

Numerical DMRG on rings up to 28 sites found a quasimetallic phase and could not resolve charge order at weak coupling (Capponi et al. 2004), placing weak coupling on the metallic side.

But

One-dimensional translation-invariant systems in the thermodynamic limit; assumes pairwise interactions.

Tools

transfer-matrix calculus (TMC) · infinite matrix product states (iMPS) · VUMPS / iDMRG · block-matrix differentiation

Abstract

Long-range interactions, from the Coulomb repulsion between electrons to the power-law interactions of trapped ions and Rydberg atoms, are widespread in quantum many-body physics. For infinite systems, however, MPS algorithms, the standard classical reference in one dimension, conventionally rely on a computational compromise: replacing these interactions by fitted sums of exponentials. We develop transfer-matrix calculus (TMC), a unified framework for deriving infinite-MPS algorithms. In TMC, an interaction is written as a function of the transfer matrix, and one set of contraction rules then yields the effective Hamiltonians of DMRG and VUMPS, the tangent-space excitation action, and the energy variance, without an MPO. Long-range interactions thus enter with their prescribed distance dependence. For the half-filled lattice Coulomb chain with a 1/d interaction of strength V, theory predicts CDW order for all V>0, but at weak coupling this order is too weak for earlier numerics to resolve. Using TMC, we obtain infinite-MPS ground states at V=2 directly in the thermodynamic limit, with an energy variance per site of 2×10⁻¹⁰. Our data, extrapolated to zero energy variance, indicate a small nonzero CDW amplitude, m₀=0.002213(14), consistent with this prediction. The complete V=2 optimization workflow across the full series of bond dimensions takes less than a day on a single AMD MI250X GPU die. For an exactly solvable long-range hopping model, TMC reproduces the nonanalytic |k| cusp of the one-particle dispersion that any fixed finite sum of decaying exponentials rounds off. We also use TMC to optimize first-quantized MPS directly in the thermodynamic limit. For half-filled free fermions, our entanglement entropy data show scaling consistent with central charge c=1 over the studied bond dimensions, as for second-quantized MPS.

item.title: QuantumInputOutput.jl: A Julia framework for input-output theory with quantum pulses and the SLH formalism
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Introduces QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source Julia framework automating symbolic derivation and numerical simulation of cascaded SLH input-output networks driven by propagating temporal quantum pulse modes via virtual cavities.

Grade 0.339 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Christoph Hotter, Orjan Ameye, Klaus Mølmer

Figure

Schematic workflow of QuantumInputOutput.jl, progressing from symbolic SLH definition and pulse mode setup to numerical Lindblad master equations or symbolic mean-field ODEs.

Asks

How can the derivation of effective Hamiltonians and Lindblad operators for open quantum systems driven by propagating temporal pulse modes across multi-component networks be automated?

But

Restricted to systems where propagating field is concentrated in a small number of discrete temporal modes; less efficient for broad multimode continua or strong temporal entanglement.

Tools

virtual-cavity input-output theory · SLH composition formalism · symbolic quantum algebra · Lindblad master-equation solvers · second-order cumulant expansion

Abstract

The interaction of traveling photonic pulses with quantum systems is a fundamental process for many quantum technologies such as quantum communication, control, and measurement protocols. The so-called SLH formalism, named for the triple of operators that parametrize the dynamics, in combination with virtual emission and absorption cavities provides a general toolbox to describe such processes. However, modeling open quantum systems driven by propagating quantum pulses becomes cumbersome once several components, channels, and temporal modes are involved. Here we present QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source framework that automates this derivation process: first, symbolic expressions for the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are derived using predefined SLH rules and symbolic quantum algebra. Next, the obtained operators are converted to (time-dependent) numerical matrices or are used to obtain higher-order mean-field equations. The numerical expressions are presented in a form immediately suitable for solving the time evolution of the master equation and analyzing the output modes via correlation functions. Besides its usefulness for numerical simulations, the framework also provides a convenient tool to derive symbolic expressions for one-dimensional quantum systems such as multilevel emitters in cavities or waveguides.

item.title: Real-time simulation of scattering in φ⁴ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Joint optimization of a single-site interpolating operator and a single-particle momentum superposition yields localized excitations that prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent from the interacting vacuum, avoiding ansatz-dependent barren plateaus.

Grade 0.336 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Boyu Gao, Natalie Klco

Figure

Eigenmodes of the wave packet momentum space profile h(k~) (left) and spatial profiles of the resulting localized excitation and wide wave packet prepared from the interacting vacuum (right). Infidelity is plotted against system size.

Asks

How can asymptotic incoming particle wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent be prepared accurately directly from the interacting vacuum in lattice field theories?

Before

Localized single-particle excitations previously required optimizing norm of excitation tensors, excess energy density with variational phases, or an ansatz for preparation circuits.

But

(1+1)-dimensional ϕ4 scalar field theory, single-site interpolating operator support, digitized local field space.

Tools

matrix product states (MPS) · quasiparticle ansatz · Lorentz symmetry phase calibration · Haag-Ruelle scattering theory

Abstract

Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in φ⁴ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulation of scattering.
